text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- After a year in office, Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson has failed to halve unemployment. The number of unemployed has actually risen during the year by one percentage point, or 32,000 people, to total 564,000 jobless.

- The Stockholm Olympics 2004 bid foundation is awaiting the results of the International Olympics Committee about its bid to host the 2004 summer games. Several foreign journalists say Stockholm has a good chance of reaching the final round along with other favourites Athens, Rome, Buenos Aires and Cape Town.

- Sweden's ruling Social Democrats continue to lose voter support, a new poll shows. Usually loyal Social Democrat voters, such as low paid or uneducated Swedes, blue collar workers, women and pensioners, have left the party. Support for the Social Democrats has fallen to 26.5 percent of voters from 45 percent at the time of the 1994 general election while support for the conservative Moderate party has risen to 32 percent from 22.5 percent, showed the survey of 1,552 people in Feruary and March this year.
- A continued strong dollar keeps lifting European stock markets. In Stockholm, engineering and forestry shares have been the winners.

- A commentary by Social Democrat Tord Andnor shows a typical view about the party in blue collar communities for the European Union's monetary union (EMU). There is mistrust and apathy for the project. Another reason is concern about that a European central bank would prioritise low inflation over lowering employment.
- Job retraining programmes seldom lead to employment, a poll by the labour board shows. Only two of 10 educated in such job schemes have found employement three months after such programmes.
- Swedish stock market analysts and fund managers forecast a continued rise in share prices.

- Central Stockholm retailers may be required to pay higher taxes if the government decides to finance a highway project around the city with higher property taxes. One boutique in the city, for example, will have to pay 50,000 more crown per year.
- The Stockholm Stock Exchange has set closing records three days running. The general index has risen 3.7 percent in four days.

- Medical and industrial gas company AGA managing director Lennart Selander said in an interview the company is not considering moving its head office abroad. There are advantages to staying in Sweden, he says.

- Swedish public telephone company Telia is losing about 200 million crowns annually on its interconnect traffic agreement with competitor Telenordia, which allows subscribers to use other telephone operators. It has renegotiated some of its agreements of this type because of the losses it made on the terms.

- Vehicle maker AB Volvo unveiled its new bus design, the B7R, to journalists in Cape Town, South Africa. Volvo Bus president Bjorn Larsson said the company would start manufacturing the model in Boras, Sweden, and then sell it to South Africa, Morocco and China.
- Stockholm still has the fastest rising rents for commercial space in Europe, a report from international property consultants Jones Lang Wootton showed. Dublin and London placed second and third.

- State owned holding company Securum is negotiating the sale of SwedShip, a ship building group which consists of three shipyards with 1996 sales of 120 million crowns. Swedish defence industries group Celsius is seen as a likely bidder. Head of negotiations at Securum, Samuel Martinsson, said he prefers to sell Swedship as a whole but Securum has received bids for the whole thing as well as for the separate companies.
